title: How to recover an unsaved document in Word on Mac: six checks for Microsoft 365
metaTitle: How to Recover an Unsaved Word Document on Mac: Steps
description: Learn how to recover an unsaved document in Word on Mac: reopen Word, check AutoRecover in Finder, then try Version History and the Trash.
targetKeyword: how to recover an unsaved document in word on mac
intro: To recover an unsaved document in Word on Mac, reopen Word first, since it usually restores its AutoRecover copy after a crash. If that does not work, check AutoSave, the hidden AutoRecover folder in Finder, Browse Version History and the Trash, in that order.
tldr: Reopen Word first. An up-to-date copy usually reopens the AutoRecover version after a crash.
Look in the hidden AutoRecover folder. Use Finder > Go > Go to Folder, or press Shift+⌘+G, then type the full path.
AutoSave and Browse Version History only work for files stored in OneDrive or SharePoint.
Choosing Don't Save on close deletes the AutoRecover file. Avoid that choice if you still need the text.
Check the Trash for a Recovered Items folder, then your Time Machine backup if you have one.

blocks.text: Why reopening Word is the first thing to try

Word keeps a background copy of the document you are editing. When Word quits unexpectedly, that copy is your best chance. Reopening Word is the cheapest test, and it takes less time than any folder search.

An up-to-date copy of Word normally reopens the AutoRecover version by itself after a crash. Microsoft's archived Learn page says Word searches for AutoRecover files every time it starts. That page is written for Windows, so your screens may look a little different. The behavior is the part that carries over.
Reopening will not help if you quit on purpose and chose Don't Save, because that choice deletes the AutoRecover copy. In that case, skip ahead to the Trash and your backups.
Check AutoSave and learn what it cannot save

AutoSave is a switch in the upper-left corner of the Word window. Microsoft says it is on by default for files stored on OneDrive, OneDrive for Business, or SharePoint Online. It is off for local folders on your Mac, for file servers, and for files you have never saved.

That last point matters most when you lost a brand-new document. AutoSave does nothing for a file that was never saved to a cloud location. If you typed a report into a blank page and Word closed, the AutoRecover folder is your best chance, and AutoSave is not part of the answer.

AutoSave also needs a Microsoft 365 subscription and the latest Word for Microsoft 365. It does not work with older .doc files. If your file is an older .doc, AutoSave will not protect it, so check the file type before you assume it is safe.
Find the AutoRecover folder without guessing

The AutoRecover folder is hidden inside your Library. Finder does not show it when you browse normally, which is why the full path has to be typed. Use your short user name, the one that sits in your home folder. It is not always the same as your full name.

Expect a mix of file names and dates. Sort by date, not by name, and compare the times with when you were working. Microsoft notes that a manual save clears earlier AutoRecover files. That means the copies you find may start at your last manual save, not at the beginning of your draft.

If Word will not open a copy, the TextEdit route in the steps is the fallback. You may lose formatting that way, so plan to reapply headings and fonts afterward. The text is what you are trying to save, so start there.
Check version history for a file you saved once

Version history helps only if the file has a home in OneDrive or SharePoint. Microsoft says version history works only for files stored there. A file on your Desktop has no version list to browse, even if you saved it many times.

The number of versions you can get back depends on the account. Personal Microsoft accounts keep the last 25 versions. Work or school accounts depend on how the library is configured, so ask your IT team if the list looks short.

This route is the right one when Word crashed after your last save and you kept typing. The version you need is usually the one from the last save, not the text you typed afterward. Expect to combine the two.
Recover a file that will not open

Sometimes the file is not missing. It is damaged, and Word refuses to open it or shows garbled text. Microsoft's fix is a setting that asks Word to confirm the file format when you open a file, then the Recover Text option.
The setting lives in Preferences, not in the File menu, so look under Word first. Once it is on, the Open dialog has a menu for the file format. Pick Recover Text there for the damaged file.
Recover Text pulls out the words. Tables, images and some formatting may not survive, so read the result carefully. Keep the damaged original untouched in case you need to try another method.
Look in the Trash and your backups
Deleted files go to the Trash. Macworld suggests looking for a folder named Recovered Items there. If you emptied the Trash, that route is gone, so check it before you empty anything else.

Time Machine is the other safety net. If it was running, a backup from before the loss may hold an older copy of the document. The catch is the gap. Anything typed after the last backup is not in it, so a backup helps with drafts more than with the last hour.

blocks.text: How often Word saves a recovery copy on Mac

The default interval is 10 minutes, according to Microsoft. That means up to ten minutes of typing may not be in the recovery copy when Word stops unexpectedly. A shorter interval means less lost work, at the cost of more frequent background saves.

To change the interval, open Word > Preferences > Save and set Save AutoRecover info. Macworld gives the path as Word > Preferences > Output and Sharing > Save. Check which one your Word shows, since menu labels change between releases.

Microsoft's archived Windows guide recommends five minutes or less for documents opened from a local disk or network share. That is a reasonable target on a Mac too if you write long documents. You can also change where AutoRecover files are stored, under Word > Preferences > Personal Settings > File Locations > AutoRecover files > Modify.

blocks.title: Menus may differ
blocks.text: Menu names here come from Microsoft and Macworld pages, not from a live copy of Word. Your version may show slightly different labels. Look for the closest match under the same menu before you assume a step is wrong.
Which Word version you are on, and why it matters

Microsoft's Mac release notes list Word version 16.114.3, Build 26102720, dated October 27, 2026. The notes describe quality and performance improvements and do not mention AutoRecover or menu changes.

To see your own version, open Word > About Word. If your build is older than the one in those notes, update Word before you rely on the recovery steps. Your build number will likely differ from the example, and that alone does not mean something is wrong.
The steps on this page target Microsoft 365 for Mac. Perpetual Office versions may behave differently, so check the support page for the version you run.
Mistakes that delete the copy you need

Three habits remove recovery copies. Choosing Don't Save on close deletes the AutoRecover file. A manual save clears earlier AutoRecover files. Emptying the Trash removes anything Word or macOS moved there, including a Recovered Items folder.

The other mistake is waiting. The longer you go without looking, the more time you spend guessing which copy is which. Search the folder, the Trash and any backup in one sitting, while the dates are still fresh in your head.
Worked example: an hour of writing with no save

Say you wrote a report in a new Word document for about an hour, and Word froze. You force quit, reopen Word, and no recovered document appears. The document was never saved, so the order changes a little.

Start with the AutoRecover folder, since the file never reached a cloud location. Sort by date and open the newest copy. If it is from about ten minutes before the freeze, expect to rewrite the last ten minutes, because the default background interval is 10 minutes.

If the folder is empty, check the Trash for Recovered Items and your Time Machine backup. The backup will not have the hour you wrote, but it may hold an earlier draft. Then shorten the AutoRecover interval before you keep writing, so the next freeze costs less.
What to do if nothing turns up

Accept that some work may be gone. Microsoft's pages describe where Word keeps copies, but they do not promise a copy in every case. Write down what you remember while it is fresh. Headings and section order are the fastest parts to rebuild from memory.

Then set up safeguards so the next loss is smaller. Save new documents to OneDrive or SharePoint, keep AutoRecover on, and set the interval to five minutes or less. Those three changes shrink the window of lost work the most.

faq.question: Can I recover a Word document I never saved on Mac?
faq.answer: Sometimes. Word keeps a background AutoRecover copy, so check the hidden AutoRecover folder first. If Word quit before any copy was written, there may be nothing to find. Microsoft's pages do not promise a copy in every case.

faq.question: Why is AutoSave not saving my new Word document?
faq.answer: AutoSave only runs on files in OneDrive, OneDrive for Business, or SharePoint Online. It is off for local folders and for files you have never saved. Move the file to OneDrive or SharePoint first if you want AutoSave to protect it.

faq.question: How often does Word save a recovery copy on Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft says the default is 10 minutes. You can change it under Word > Preferences > Save. Macworld lists Word > Preferences > Output and Sharing > Save, so check which path your version shows.

faq.question: Does clicking Don't Save delete the recovery copy?
faq.answer: Yes, according to Microsoft. Choosing Don't Save on close deletes the AutoRecover file. If you are unsure, choose Cancel and save the document first.

faq.question: What if Word will not open my AutoRecover file?
faq.answer: Macworld suggests opening the file in TextEdit by dragging it onto the TextEdit icon in the Dock. Then copy the text into a new Word document. Formatting may need to be reapplied after you paste it.

faq.question: Can I use version history for a file on my Desktop?
faq.answer: No. Microsoft says version history works only for files stored in OneDrive or SharePoint. A local file has no version list to browse, so look in the AutoRecover folder and your Time Machine backup instead.

faq.question: How do I recover an older version in Word for the web?
faq.answer: Open the file, choose File > Version History, select a version, and select Restore. Microsoft's pages I checked do not cover recovering an unsaved document in Word for the web.

faq.question: How many versions can I get back?
faq.answer: Personal Microsoft accounts keep the last 25 versions. Work or school accounts depend on how the library is set up, so ask your IT team if the list looks shorter than expected.

steps.name: Reopen Word and let it look for a copy
steps.text: Quit Word if it is frozen, then open it again from the Dock or the Applications folder. When Word starts, it searches for AutoRecover copies. A copy normally reopens by itself after a crash, so look at the window before you do anything else.
steps.tip: If Word opens to a blank page, keep going with the next steps before you type anything new.

steps.name: Check the AutoSave switch in the window
steps.text: Look at the upper-left corner of the Word window for the AutoSave switch. It only works for files stored on OneDrive, OneDrive for Business, or SharePoint Online. For a file on your Mac, or a file you have never saved, it stays off.
steps.tip: To keep AutoSave for future work, save the document in a OneDrive or SharePoint location from the start.

steps.name: Open the AutoRecover folder in Finder
steps.text: Click the Finder icon in the Dock, then choose Go > Go to Folder or press Shift+⌘+G. Type this path, replacing <username> with your short Mac user name, then press Return: /Users/<username>/Library/Containers/com.Microsoft.Word/Data/Library/Preferences/AutoRecovery
steps.tip: The Library folder is hidden. Typing the full path is the only reliable way in, so copy it exactly.

steps.name: Find the newest copy and open it in Word
steps.text: Sort the folder by date modified, then start with the copy closest to when the work went missing. Open it in Word and read the text. A manual save removes earlier AutoRecover files, so the copy you find may begin at your last save.
steps.tip: Use File > Save As to keep the recovered text in a file with a clear name.

steps.name: Use Browse Version History for a saved file
steps.text: If you saved the file at least once and it lives in OneDrive or SharePoint, click the document name in the title bar and choose Browse Version History. Older Office for Mac versions use File > Browse Version History instead. Selecting a version opens it in a separate window.
steps.tip: Personal Microsoft accounts keep the last 25 versions. Work or school accounts depend on the library settings.

steps.name: Copy the text you need from the old version
steps.text: Scroll through the version in its separate window, find the paragraph you need, and copy it into your current document. The Mac steps describe opening a version in its own window, so copy from there. Word for the web works differently, as the FAQ explains.
steps.tip: Keep the version window open while you paste, so you do not lose your place in the older text.

steps.name: Turn on the setting that opens damaged files
steps.text: Open Word > Preferences > Authoring and Proofing Tools > General. Select Confirm file format conversion at Open, then close the Preferences window. Recover Text is only useful after this setting is on.
steps.tip: This step is for files that will not open cleanly. It does not bring back text you never saved.

steps.name: Open the damaged file with Recover Text
steps.text: Choose File > Open, then pick Recover Text from the menu at the bottom right of the dialog. Select the damaged document and open it. Check the result line by line, because tables, images and some formatting may not come back.
steps.tip: Work on a copy of the damaged file, so the original stays as it was.

steps.name: Check the Trash for a Recovered Items folder
steps.text: Open the Trash from the Dock and look for a folder named Recovered Items. Macworld suggests checking here, since deleted or moved files can end up in the Trash. Do not empty the Trash until you have searched it.
steps.tip: Emptying the Trash removes everything in it, so search there before you empty it.

steps.name: Check Time Machine for an older copy
steps.text: If you use Time Machine, open it and browse back to a time before the loss. Find the folder the file lived in, then open the document from that backup. Anything typed after the last backup will not be there.
steps.tip: A backup can hold an older draft even when the newest text is gone.

steps.name: Copy text out of a file Word will not open
steps.text: Open TextEdit. Drag the AutoRecover file onto the TextEdit icon in the Dock. Copy the text, then paste it into a new Word document. Macworld also mentions opening the temporary folder from Terminal with open $TMPDIR, if you need to look further.
steps.tip: You may lose formatting this way. Reapply headings and fonts once the text is back in Word.

shortcuts.action: Go to Folder in Finder, to type the AutoRecover path

troubleshooting.problem: The AutoRecover folder is missing or empty
troubleshooting.fix: Check that the path uses your short user name. If the folder exists but is empty, a manual save or a Don't Save choice may have cleared the copy. Move on to the Trash and Time Machine.

troubleshooting.problem: Menu names do not match the steps
troubleshooting.fix: Menu names come from Microsoft and Macworld pages. Look for the closest match under the same menu. Compare your build under Word > About Word with 16.114.3.
Version history needs a file stored in OneDrive or SharePoint. Save a copy there and check again. Work and school accounts depend on admin settings.
Both Recover Text and the TextEdit route can strip formatting. Reapply headings and fonts, and compare the text with any other copy you find.

troubleshooting.problem: AutoSave does not run on an older file
troubleshooting.fix: AutoSave does not work with older .doc files. Save the document as a newer Word file in OneDrive or SharePoint to use AutoSave.

troubleshooting.problem: Word will not open the damaged file
troubleshooting.fix: Turn on Confirm file format conversion at Open under Word > Preferences > Authoring and Proofing Tools > General. Then open the file with Recover Text from File > Open.
